Bergamot.source: Cold-pressed from the peel of the bergamot orange. About 80% of the world's supply grows on a narrow strip of coast around Reggio Calabria in southern Italy.
Bergamot.history: Grown in Calabria since the 1700s, bergamot became the heart of the original Eau de Cologne made by Giovanni Maria Farina in Cologne in 1709. Today perfumers use a 'bergapten-free' version, with the compound that makes skin sensitive to sunlight removed.

Lemon.source: Cold-pressed from lemon peel, mainly in Argentina, Sicily and Spain.
Lemon.history: The lemon came from the foothills of the Himalayas and reached the Mediterranean with Arab traders around the 10th century. It was one of the key citrus oils in the 18th-century colognes.

Mandarin Orange.source: Cold-pressed from mandarin peel, mostly in Sicily, Brazil and China. Green, yellow and red oils are pressed at different stages of ripeness.
Mandarin Orange.history: Native to China, the fruit takes its name from the mandarins, officials of the imperial court. It reached Europe only in the early 1800s.
molecules: the sweet, juicy signature of mandarin

Orange.source: Sweet orange oil is cold-pressed from the peel, a by-product of the juice industry in Brazil and Florida.
Orange.history: Portuguese traders brought the sweet orange from Asia to Europe in the 15th and 16th centuries, and orangeries became a status symbol for European royalty.
molecules: makes up about 95% of the oil: sunny orange peel

Grapefruit.source: Cold-pressed from the peel, mainly in the USA, Israel and South Africa. Its key molecule, nootkatone, is often made by fermentation.
Grapefruit.history: Grapefruit is a natural cross between pomelo and sweet orange that appeared in 18th-century Barbados, where it was called the 'forbidden fruit'.
molecules: a sulphur molecule so strong it's smelled in parts per trillion

Lime.source: Pressed or steam-distilled from limes in Mexico and Peru. Distilled lime oil is the classic cola flavour.
Lime.history: Limes came from Southeast Asia. In the 19th century the British navy gave sailors lime juice against scurvy, which is how they got the nickname 'limeys'.
molecules: the sweet 'lime candy' note of distilled lime

Yuzu.source: Pressed from the peel of yuzu fruit grown in Japan (especially Kochi) and Korea. The oil is rare and costly, so most yuzu notes are recreated.
Yuzu.history: Yuzu came to Japan from China more than a thousand years ago. On the winter solstice, people still take baths with whole yuzu floating in the water.

Neroli.source: Steam-distilled from the white blossoms of the bitter orange tree in Tunisia, Morocco, Egypt and the south of France. It takes about a tonne of flowers to make one kilo of oil.
Neroli.history: It's named after Anne-Marie Orsini, princess of Nerola, who used it to scent her gloves and baths in the late 1600s, making it fashionable in Europe.
molecules: a grape-like sweetness typical of orange flowers

Petitgrain.source: Steam-distilled from the leaves and twigs of the bitter orange tree, mainly in Paraguay and around the Mediterranean.
Petitgrain.history: Its name means 'little grain', because it was first distilled from small, unripe oranges. It has been a classic of colognes since the 18th century.

Rose.source: Damask rose is grown in Bulgaria's Valley of Roses and in Isparta, Turkey. The May rose (Rosa centifolia) is grown around Grasse and in Morocco. About 3,500 kg of petals make 1 kg of rose oil.
Rose.history: The Persian physician Ibn Sina (Avicenna) refined the steam distillation of rose water around the year 1000. Bulgaria has produced rose oil since the 17th century.
molecules: tiny amounts give a jammy, fruity depth

Jasmine.source: The flowers are picked by hand at dawn and solvent-extracted into an absolute, mainly in India and Egypt, with a little still grown around Grasse.
Jasmine.history: Jasmine has been grown around Grasse since the 17th century and became the signature flower of French perfumery. In 1962 Firmenich created Hedione, a synthetic molecule inspired by jasmine.

Tuberose.source: Solvent-extracted from the flowers, today mainly in Tamil Nadu, India. It's one of the most expensive floral absolutes.
Tuberose.history: The Aztecs grew it in Mexico. Spanish explorers brought it to Europe in the 16th century, and it was grown around Grasse for centuries.

Ylang-Ylang.source: Steam-distilled from the flowers in the Comoros, Madagascar and Mayotte. The distillation is split into grades from 'Extra' (the first and finest) to 'III'.
Ylang-Ylang.history: The name comes from Tagalog in the Philippines. The French planted it in Réunion and the Comoros in the late 1800s, and it became famous in Chanel No 5 (1921).

Iris.source: From the rhizomes (roots) of iris grown around Florence. The roots are dried for three years before distillation into 'orris butter', which can cost more than gold by weight.
Iris.history: Orris root powder scented linen and wigs in Renaissance Europe, and the iris is the emblem of Florence. Its smell only develops as the root slowly ages.
molecules: powdery, violet-like, slightly woody: formed as the root ages
odourless, it makes orris oil solid like butter

Violet.source: Real violet flower oil is almost impossible to make, so violet is recreated with ionones.
Violet.history: In 1893 the chemists Ferdinand Tiemann and Paul Krüger made the first ionones. Violet scents became a craze, especially Parma violets grown around Toulouse.
molecules: violet with a woody, raspberry edge

Violet Leaf.source: Solvent-extracted from violet leaves grown in France and Egypt.
Violet Leaf.history: Violet leaf became a modern classic of 'green' masculine perfumes such as Grey Flannel (1975) and Dior's Fahrenheit (1988).

Lavender.source: Steam-distilled from the flowering tops, mainly in Haute-Provence in France and in Bulgaria (now the biggest producer).
Lavender.history: The Romans scented their baths with it (its name comes from Latin 'lavare', to wash). In 1882 Houbigant's Fougère Royale paired lavender with coumarin and created the fougère family.

Lily of the Valley.source: A 'mute' flower: no usable oil can be extracted, so its scent is always recreated by perfumers.
Lily of the Valley.history: Edmond Roudnitska made the definitive lily of the valley perfume, Dior's Diorissimo, in 1956. Several classic lily-of-the-valley molecules (Lilial, Lyral) have since been banned in the EU as allergens.

Orange Blossom.source: Solvent-extracted from bitter orange flowers in Tunisia, Morocco and Egypt. The same flowers give neroli when steam-distilled.
Orange Blossom.history: Orange flower water has been made in the Mediterranean and Middle East for centuries. Brides wore orange blossom in Europe as a symbol of purity.

Osmanthus.source: Solvent-extracted from tiny flowers in China, especially around Guilin, whose name means 'forest of sweet osmanthus'.
Osmanthus.history: In China osmanthus has flavoured tea, wine and sweets for centuries. It became a niche-perfume favourite for its apricot-and-leather smell.

Gardenia.source: Gardenia gives almost no extract, so perfumers rebuild its smell from other materials.
Gardenia.history: The plant was named in 1761 after Alexander Garden, a Scottish-American naturalist. It is native to southern China and Japan.

Magnolia.source: Most magnolia oil comes from the white champaca (Michelia alba) grown in China. Large magnolia blooms are usually recreated.
Magnolia.history: Magnolia is named after the French botanist Pierre Magnol. It is one of the oldest flowering plants on Earth, older than bees.

Peony.source: Peony flowers give no usable oil, so peony is an accord built by the perfumer.
Peony.history: In China the peony has been called the 'king of flowers' since the Tang dynasty. It became a perfume favourite in the 2000s.

Geranium.source: Steam-distilled from the leaves of rose-scented pelargonium in Egypt, China and Réunion (the prized 'Bourbon' geranium).
Geranium.history: The plant came to Europe from South Africa in the 17th century. French perfumers first distilled it in 1819, as a cheaper way to get a rose-like oil.

Immortelle.source: Steam-distilled or extracted from the yellow flowers in Corsica and the Balkans.
Immortelle.history: Its name means 'everlasting', because the flowers keep their colour when dried. Corsican immortelle is prized for its smell of honey, hay and curry.
molecules: the warm curry and maple-syrup note

Heliotrope.source: The flower isn't extracted. Its almond-and-vanilla smell is made with the molecule heliotropin.
Heliotrope.history: The botanist Joseph de Jussieu sent heliotrope seeds from Peru to Paris in the 1740s. Guerlain used heliotropin in L'Heure Bleue (1912).

Mimosa.source: Solvent-extracted from the yellow flowers and twigs, mainly in the Tanneron hills near Grasse.
Mimosa.history: Mimosa came from Australia and was planted on the French Riviera in the 19th century. Every February the region holds mimosa festivals.

Saffron.source: From the dried red stigmas of the saffron crocus, mainly in Iran, Kashmir and Spain. Perfumes usually use synthetic saffron notes.
Saffron.history: Minoan frescoes on Santorini (around 1600 BCE) already show saffron gatherers. It takes about 150,000 flowers to make a kilo of the spice.
molecules: leathery, hay-like saffron, formed as the stigmas dry

Pink Pepper.source: Distilled or CO2-extracted from the pink berries of the Peruvian pepper tree, in Réunion, Madagascar and Peru. It isn't a true pepper.
Pink Pepper.history: The Incas used the tree for medicine and drinks. Pink pepper became fashionable in perfume in the 1990s and 2000s as a rosy, sparkling spice.

Pepper.source: Steam-distilled or CO2-extracted from black peppercorns from India's Malabar coast and Vietnam.
Pepper.history: Pepper was once so valuable it was called 'black gold' and used to pay rents. It drove the spice trade between India, Arabia and Rome.

Sichuan Pepper.source: From the dried husks of prickly-ash berries grown in Sichuan, China.
Sichuan Pepper.history: Used in Chinese cooking and medicine for over 2,000 years. Its tingle on the tongue comes from sanshool, which has no smell.

Cardamom.source: Steam-distilled from the seeds, mostly in Guatemala and southern India.
Cardamom.history: Cardamom grows wild in the forests of India's Western Ghats. Vikings brought it to Scandinavia, where it still flavours sweet buns.

Cinnamon.source: Distilled from the bark or leaves of the cinnamon tree in Sri Lanka, or from cassia bark in China.
Cinnamon.history: Ancient Egyptians used cinnamon in embalming. Arab traders told tall tales about where it came from to protect their monopoly.

Clove.source: Distilled from the dried flower buds (and leaves) of the clove tree, in Madagascar, Zanzibar and Indonesia.
Clove.history: Cloves came only from the Maluku 'Spice Islands' for centuries. In 1770 the Frenchman Pierre Poivre smuggled seedlings out, breaking the Dutch monopoly.
molecules: about 80% of the oil: warm, spicy, dentist-like

Nutmeg.source: Steam-distilled from the seeds of the nutmeg tree, in Indonesia and Grenada.
Nutmeg.history: Nutmeg came only from the tiny Banda Islands. In 1667 the Dutch kept the nutmeg island of Run and let the English keep Manhattan.

Ginger.source: Steam-distilled or CO2-extracted from the rhizome, in India, China and Nigeria.
Ginger.history: Ginger has been used in Asian medicine for thousands of years, and was one of the first spices to reach Europe via the spice trade.

Elemi.source: Steam-distilled from the resin of a tree native to the Philippines.
Elemi.history: Elemi resin was used in ointments and varnishes from the 15th century, and in incense in churches. Perfumers love its lemon-and-pepper incense.

Sandalwood.source: Steam-distilled from the heartwood of trees at least 15 years old. Indian (Mysore) sandalwood is now rare, so most comes from Australian plantations or is synthetic.
Sandalwood.history: Sandalwood has been used in Indian temples and rituals for over 4,000 years. Overharvesting in the 20th century led to synthetics like Javanol and Ebanol.

Cedar.source: Steam-distilled from wood chips. Virginia and Texas 'cedar' (actually junipers) come from the USA, and Atlas cedar from Morocco.
Cedar.history: Ancient Egyptians used cedar oil in mummification. Cedarwood is the smell of pencils, which were long made from Virginia cedar.

Vetiver.source: Distilled from the roots of a tall grass, mainly in Haiti, Java and Réunion.
Vetiver.history: In India 'khus' mats woven from vetiver roots are dampened to cool houses with their scent. Vetiver became a men's classic with Guerlain's Vetiver (1959).

Patchouli.source: Distilled from dried, lightly fermented leaves, about 90% in Indonesia (Sulawesi).
Patchouli.history: In the 19th century, Indian shawls were packed in patchouli leaves to keep moths away, so Europeans linked the smell with luxury. It became the scent of the 1960s hippies.
molecules: the true 'patchouli' smell, found in tiny amounts

Oud.source: When Aquilaria trees in South and Southeast Asia are infected by a mould, they make a dark, fragrant resin called agarwood. Real oud oil is extremely costly, so most perfumes use an 'oud accord'.
Oud.history: Agarwood is mentioned in ancient Sanskrit texts and burned in the Japanese incense ceremony (kōdō). It entered Western perfumery with YSL's M7 in 2002.
molecules: the smoky-sweet smell released when agarwood is heated

Akigalawood.source: A Givaudan material made by treating a fraction of patchouli oil with an enzyme. This 'biotech' process creates new peppery, oud-like molecules.
Akigalawood.history: Akigalawood was launched by Givaudan in the 2010s as a sustainable way to give the smoky, spicy feel of oud.

Guaiac Wood.source: Steam-distilled from the wood of a tree from the Gran Chaco region of Paraguay and Argentina.
Guaiac Wood.history: Guaiac wood oil entered perfumery in the late 19th century. Its smoky, rosy wood is a classic in leather and oriental perfumes.

Cashmeran.source: A synthetic molecule made in the lab. It doesn't exist in nature.
Cashmeran.history: Created at IFF around 1970 by the chemist John Hall. Its name evokes the softness of cashmere.
molecules: musky, woody, spicy and slightly fruity: like warm skin in a wool jumper

Iso E Super.source: A synthetic woody molecule made in the lab.
Iso E Super.history: Discovered at IFF in 1973 by John Hall and James Sanders. Escentric Molecules' Molecule 01 (2006) was made of nothing but Iso E Super, and it's the backbone of Terre d'Hermès.
molecules: velvety, cedar-like wood that feels like skin
a tiny, very powerful isomer that carries most of the smell

Cypress.source: Steam-distilled from the twigs and needles of the Mediterranean cypress in France, Spain and Morocco.
Cypress.history: The cypress has been a symbol of mourning and eternity since ancient Greece. It's planted in cemeteries across the Mediterranean.

Birch.source: Birch tar is made by heating birch bark without air, then refining the tar. It's used in tiny doses for a smoky leather note.
Birch.history: Russian leather was tanned with birch tar, giving it a famous smell. Chanel's Cuir de Russie (1924) recreated it as a perfume.

Vanilla.source: From cured pods of a climbing orchid, about 80% from Madagascar. Most vanilla notes are made with synthetic vanillin.
Vanilla.history: The Totonac people of Mexico grew vanilla long before the Aztecs. In 1841, 12-year-old Edmond Albius on Réunion discovered how to pollinate it by hand, and vanillin was first synthesised in 1874.
molecules: a light smoky touch in real vanilla pods

Tonka Bean.source: Seeds of a large tree from Venezuela and Brazil. The beans are soaked in rum and dried, then extracted.
Tonka Bean.history: Coumarin was isolated from tonka beans in 1820 and synthesised by William Henry Perkin in 1868. Houbigant's Fougère Royale (1882) was one of the first perfumes to use a synthetic molecule.

Benzoin.source: Resin tapped from styrax trees in Laos and Thailand (Siam benzoin) or Sumatra.
Benzoin.history: Its name comes from the Arabic for 'frankincense of Java'. It's been burned as incense for centuries and is a key part of Guerlain's Shalimar.

Labdanum.source: A sticky resin from rockrose bushes in Andalusia, Spain, and Crete.
Labdanum.history: The Greek historian Herodotus described labdanum being combed from the beards of goats that grazed on rockrose. It's the heart of most 'amber' accords.

Amber.source: Not fossilised amber, which barely smells. In perfume 'amber' is an accord, usually of labdanum, vanilla and benzoin.
Amber.history: Coty's Ambre Antique (1905) was one of the first amber perfumes, followed by Guerlain's Shalimar (1925). The 'oriental' or 'amber' family grew from them.

Ambroxan.source: Made from sclareol, a molecule from clary sage, or by fermentation. It also forms naturally in ambergris.
Ambroxan.history: Firmenich created Ambrox in 1950 to replace costly ambergris. Ambroxan became famous through Molecule 02 and Dior's Sauvage (2015).
molecules: dry, salty, woody amber that clings to skin

Ambergris.source: A waxy substance made in the gut of sperm whales and found washed up on beaches, after years ageing in the sea. Today it's mostly replaced by synthetics.
Ambergris.history: Medieval Arab traders valued it above gold. It was used to make perfumes last longer, and is now restricted in many countries.
molecules: odourless itself, it breaks down in sunlight and seawater
the dry, ambery-woody product of that breakdown

Incense.source: Frankincense (olibanum) is resin tapped from Boswellia trees in Oman, Yemen and Somalia, then distilled.
Incense.history: Around 1470 BCE Queen Hatshepsut of Egypt sent an expedition to the land of Punt to bring back incense trees. Frankincense was one of the gifts of the Magi.

Myrrh.source: Resin from thorny Commiphora trees in Somalia, Ethiopia and Yemen.
Myrrh.history: Ancient Egyptians used myrrh in embalming and in the incense 'kyphi'. Like frankincense, it was one of the gifts of the Magi.
molecules: the warm, medicinal-balsamic smell of myrrh

Honey.source: Beeswax absolute gives a natural honey smell, but most honey notes are made with synthetic molecules.
Honey.history: Honey and beeswax were among the earliest perfume materials. Egyptians used beeswax as a base for scented cones worn on the head.
molecules: honey, with a slightly animalic edge

Caramel.source: Built with synthetic molecules that smell of burnt sugar.
Caramel.history: Thierry Mugler's Angel (1992) used a big dose of ethyl maltol and created the 'gourmand' family, perfumes that smell edible.

Coffee.source: CO2 extract of roasted coffee beans. Coffee notes are often boosted with synthetic molecules.
Coffee.history: The roasting smell comes from hundreds of molecules formed when beans are heated. Mugler's A*Men (1996) made coffee a perfume note.

Cocoa.source: Absolute or CO2 extract of roasted cocoa beans, mainly from West Africa and South America.
Cocoa.history: The Olmecs of Mexico drank cocoa over 3,500 years ago. Its smell develops only when the beans are fermented and roasted.

Praline.source: An accord of caramel and roasted nuts.
Praline.history: Praline is named after the 17th-century Duke of Choiseul-Praslin, whose cook made sugar-coated almonds. Lancôme's La Vie est Belle (2012) made it a mainstream perfume note.

Almond.source: Bitter almond oil from almonds or apricot kernels. Today the almond molecule, benzaldehyde, is mostly synthetic.
Almond.history: Benzaldehyde was first extracted from bitter almonds in 1803 and made in the lab in 1832. It was one of the first molecules chemists understood.

Rum.source: Usually an accord, sometimes with rum absolute.
Rum.history: Rum was first distilled from sugar-cane molasses in 17th-century Caribbean plantations. In perfume it adds a boozy, sweet warmth.

Tobacco.source: Absolute extracted from cured tobacco leaves in Bulgaria and the USA. It contains no nicotine.
Tobacco.history: Caron's Tabac Blond (1919) was made for women who had just started smoking in public. Tobacco now appears in many warm, sweet perfumes.

Musk.source: Originally from a gland of the male musk deer, now protected. All modern musks are synthetic, apart from a few plant musks like ambrette.
Musk.history: In 1888 Albert Baur accidentally made the first synthetic musk while working on explosives. Leopold Ružička worked out the structure of muscone in 1926, and later won a Nobel Prize.

Leather.source: An accord built from smoky, tarry and animalic materials.
Leather.history: In the 16th and 17th centuries Grasse was a tanning town, and glove makers perfumed their leather to hide the smell. Perfumery in Grasse grew out of this trade.

Suede.history: Suede accords became popular in the 2000s as a softer, gentler leather. They often pair iris, saffron and musks.

Civet.source: Originally from the glands of the African civet cat in Ethiopia. Today it's replaced by synthetics for ethical reasons.
Civet.history: Civet was used in tiny amounts in classic perfumes for its warm, sensual effect. Ružička also worked out the structure of civetone in 1926.
molecules: faecal in large doses, but warm and sensual in traces

Castoreum.source: Originally from the castor sacs of beavers. Today it's recreated with synthetic molecules.
Castoreum.history: Castoreum was used in medicine since antiquity and in leather perfumes like Caron's Tabac Blond. Its smoky-leathery smell partly comes from the willow bark beavers eat.

Ozone.source: Made with synthetic molecules that evoke fresh air after a storm. Real ozone smells sharp and electric.
Ozone.history: 'Ozonic' perfumes took off in the early 1990s with fragrances like Issey Miyake's L'Eau d'Issey (1992).

Sea Notes.source: An accord of marine synthetics, sometimes with seaweed absolute.
Sea Notes.history: Aramis New West for Her (1988) and Davidoff Cool Water (1988) launched the 'marine' or 'aquatic' family.
molecules: in traces: the smell of the sea air itself

Calone.source: A synthetic molecule. It doesn't occur in nature.
Calone.history: Calone was discovered in 1966 by Pfizer chemists who were researching tranquillisers. It became the signature of the 1990s 'marine' perfumes.
molecules: fresh sea breeze with a watermelon twist

Mineral Notes.source: An accord that evokes wet stone, flint, chalk or salt.
Mineral Notes.history: Mineral accords became fashionable in niche perfumery in the 2000s, as perfumers looked for 'clean' textures that aren't flowers or woods.

Aldehydes.source: A family of molecules found in citrus peel, made synthetically for perfume.
Aldehydes.history: Ernest Beaux made aldehydes famous with an overdose in Chanel No 5 (1921), giving it its sparkling, champagne-like lift.
molecules: metallic and ambery, the No 5 sparkle

Petrichor.source: The smell of rain on dry earth. In perfume it's recreated with geosmin, or in India with 'mitti attar', distilled from baked clay.
Petrichor.history: Australian scientists Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas named it 'petrichor' in 1964. Humans can smell geosmin at about 5 parts per trillion.
molecules: wet soil, made by Streptomyces bacteria

Mint.source: Steam-distilled from peppermint and spearmint leaves, mostly in the USA and India.
Mint.history: The ancient Greeks and Romans used mint in baths and to perfume tables. Its name comes from the nymph Minthe in Greek myth.

Basil.source: Steam-distilled from the leaves and flowers, in Egypt, India and the Comoros.
Basil.history: Basil came from India, where holy basil (tulsi) is sacred. Its name comes from the Greek for 'royal'.

Rosemary.source: Steam-distilled from the leaves and flowering tops, in Tunisia, Morocco and Spain.
Rosemary.history: 'Hungary Water', one of the first alcohol-based perfumes (14th century), was made mainly from rosemary. Legend says it was made for a queen of Hungary.

Sage.source: Common sage leaves come from Dalmatia (Croatia). Clary sage, the one perfumers use most, grows in France and Russia.
Sage.history: Sage's name comes from Latin 'salvare', to heal. Clary sage is also the source of sclareol, used to make Ambrox.

Tea.source: Tea absolutes exist but are rare, so most tea notes are accords.
Tea.history: Tea has been drunk in China for at least 2,000 years. Jean-Claude Ellena's Eau Parfumée au Thé Vert for Bulgari (1992) launched tea as a perfume note.

Fig.source: Fig leaf absolute is rare, so fig is mostly an accord of green, milky and coconut notes.
Fig.history: Olivia Giacobetti created two landmark figs: Premier Figuier for L'Artisan Parfumeur (1994) and Philosykos for Diptyque (1996).

Galbanum.source: A resin from a giant fennel plant that grows in Iran.
Galbanum.history: Galbanum was part of the holy incense in the Bible (Exodus). Germaine Cellier used a record dose in Balmain's Vent Vert (1947).

Grass.source: An accord based on the molecules a plant releases when its leaves are cut.
Grass.history: Leaf alcohol (cis-3-hexenol) was identified in green tea leaves in 1933. It's the classic 'freshly mown lawn' smell.

Apple.source: Apples give no usable oil, so apple is built from fruity esters.
Apple.history: Fruity apple notes became popular in the 2000s, with perfumes like DKNY Be Delicious (2004).

Pear.history: Isoamyl acetate gives the famous 'pear drops' sweet smell. Pear became a popular fruity-floral top note in the 2000s.

Peach.source: Recreated mainly with lactones, molecules that also occur in real peaches.
Peach.history: Guerlain's Mitsouko (1919) used gamma-undecalactone, nicknamed 'aldehyde C-14', to give its famous peach skin.

Blackcurrant.source: Absolute from blackcurrant buds (bourgeons de cassis), mainly in Burgundy, France. Often boosted with synthetic sulphur molecules.
Blackcurrant.history: Burgundy has grown blackcurrants for crème de cassis since the 19th century. The buds' smell is famously 'catty'.

Raspberry.source: Recreated with raspberry ketone and ionones. Natural raspberry ketone is extremely costly.
Raspberry.history: Raspberry ketone is found in raspberries in tiny amounts. Raspberry notes became a favourite in sweet, fruity perfumes from the 1990s.

Pineapple.history: Pineapple became a perfume talking point with Creed's Aventus (2010), where it pairs with birch and musk.

Coconut.source: Recreated with lactones. Coconut absolutes exist but are faint.
Coconut.history: The coconut lactone gamma-nonalactone is nicknamed 'aldehyde C-18'. It's the smell of suncream and tropical holidays.

Cherry.history: Cherry notes became a niche trend with Tom Ford's Lost Cherry (2018).

Plum.source: Recreated with lactones and fruity molecules.
Plum.history: Rochas Femme (1944) by Edmond Roudnitska made plum famous, using a plum base called Prunol.

Oakmoss.source: Extracted from a lichen that grows on oak trees in the Balkans, France and Morocco.
Oakmoss.history: Coty's Chypre (1917) built a whole family on oakmoss, bergamot and labdanum. Since the 2000s it's been heavily restricted because of allergens.

Cumin.source: Steam-distilled from cumin seeds in India and Iran.
Cumin.history: Cumin seeds were found in ancient Egyptian tombs. In perfume, small amounts add a warm, skin-like, slightly sweaty sensuality.

Coriander.source: Steam-distilled from coriander seeds, mainly in Russia, Ukraine and Morocco.
Coriander.history: Coriander seeds were found in Tutankhamun's tomb. The seeds smell sweet and floral, very different from the leaves.
molecules: 60–80% of the oil: sweet, floral and woody

Juniper.source: Steam-distilled from juniper berries, mostly in the Balkans and Italy.
Juniper.history: Juniper was burned to purify the air during plague outbreaks. Its berries give gin its flavour.

Gin.source: An accord of juniper, coriander, citrus peel and angelica: the botanicals of gin.
Gin.history: Gin grew out of Dutch genever in the 17th century and became a London craze in the 18th. Gin notes appear in fresh, boozy perfumes.

Cypriol.source: Steam-distilled from the roots of a sedge grown in India, where it's called nagarmotha.
Cypriol.history: Cypriol has long been used in Indian attars and incense. Perfumers use it as a smoky, leathery stand-in for oud and vetiver.

Opoponax.source: Resin from 'sweet myrrh' trees in Somalia and Ethiopia.
Opoponax.history: Used in ancient incense, opoponax gives a sweet, warm, balsamic depth to oriental perfumes like Guerlain's Shalimar.

Cistus.source: Steam-distilled from the leaves and twigs of the rockrose shrub in Spain. The resin from the same plant is labdanum.
Cistus.history: Rockrose covers the hills of Andalusia and Crete. On hot days its leaves release a sticky, ambery smell.

Styrax.source: A balsam from sweetgum trees in Turkey or Central America.
Styrax.history: Styrax has been burned as incense since antiquity. Its smoky, leathery balsam is a classic in leather and amber perfumes.

Peru Balsam.source: A resin from trees in El Salvador. It was named after Peru because it was shipped from Lima in colonial times.
Peru Balsam.history: Peru balsam was used in medicine and perfume since the 16th century. Today its use is restricted because it can cause allergies.

Carnation.source: Carnation absolute is very rare. The scent is usually rebuilt with clove-like molecules.
Carnation.history: Caron's Bellodgia (1927) was a famous carnation perfume. The flower's Latin name means 'flower of the gods'.

Freesia.source: Freesia gives no oil, so it's an accord.
Freesia.history: Freesia comes from South Africa and was named in the 19th century after the German doctor Friedrich Freese. It was a hugely popular note in the 1990s.

Lily.source: Lily absolute was made in the past but is now very rare. Lily notes are usually built from other molecules.
Lily.history: The ancient Greeks made a famous lily perfume called 'susinum'. The Madonna lily has been grown for over 3,000 years.

Linden Blossom.source: Absolute from linden (lime tree) flowers, rare and costly, from France and Bulgaria. Usually an accord.
Linden Blossom.history: Linden blossom tea (tilleul) is a classic French remedy for calm and sleep. The trees line many European streets.

Hyacinth.source: Hyacinth absolute was once made in Holland and France. Today the scent is almost always recreated.
Hyacinth.history: Hyacinths were the craze of 18th-century Holland, after the tulip. In Greek myth the flower grew from the blood of the youth Hyacinthus.
molecules: green and honeyed: the hyacinth key

Narcissus.source: Absolute from wild poet's narcissus, picked in the Lozère and Aubrac regions of France.
Narcissus.history: In Greek myth Narcissus fell in love with his own reflection and turned into this flower. Its absolute smells of hay, honey and horses.

Tiare.source: Tiare flowers are soaked in coconut oil to make Monoï de Tahiti, which has had its own protected designation of origin since 1992.
Tiare.history: Polynesians have used monoï for centuries to protect skin and hair. Tiare is the national flower of Tahiti.

Orchid.source: Almost no orchids give a usable extract (vanilla is the exception), so 'orchid' is a fantasy accord.
Orchid.history: Orchid mania swept Victorian Britain. Tom Ford's Black Orchid (2006) made the orchid a perfume icon.

Hedione.source: A synthetic molecule inspired by jasmine.
Hedione.history: Firmenich chemist Edouard Demole created Hedione in 1962 after studying jasmine. Dior's Eau Sauvage (1966) was the first big perfume to use it.
molecules: airy, transparent jasmine and citrus: it makes a perfume feel radiant

Rhubarb.source: Rhubarb gives no oil, so it's recreated with green, tart molecules.
Rhubarb.history: Rhubarb became a fashionable 'tart green' note in the 2000s and 2010s.

Green Notes.source: A general term for the smell of leaves, stems and sap.
Green Notes.history: Green perfumes boomed after Balmain's Vent Vert (1947) and Chanel No 19 (1970).

Papyrus.source: Papyrus 'oil' comes from the roots of Cyperus plants, close cousins of the papyrus reed.
Papyrus.history: Ancient Egyptians made paper from papyrus reeds along the Nile. In perfume it gives a smoky, woody, slightly leathery feel.

Palo Santo.source: Distilled from fallen branches and dead trees in Ecuador and Peru.
Palo Santo.history: Its name means 'holy wood'. The Incas burned it to cleanse spaces, and it's still used in spiritual rituals.

Oak.source: Mostly an accord. Oak extracts exist, often made from toasted barrel wood.
Oak.history: Wine and whisky get much of their smell from ageing in oak barrels. Perfumers borrow the same molecules.

Woody Notes.source: A general term for the smell of woods, natural or synthetic.
Woody Notes.history: Woody notes are the base of most masculine perfumes. Synthetic woods like Iso E Super changed how modern perfumes smell.

Fir.source: Distilled from the needles of fir trees, or extracted from fir balsam, in Canada and Europe.
Fir.history: Fir is the Christmas tree smell. Fir balsam absolute has a jammy, almost fruity sweetness.

Pine.source: Steam-distilled from Scots pine needles and twigs.
Pine.history: Pine has been used in baths and medicine for centuries. It became the classic 'clean' smell of 20th-century household products.

Amberwood.source: A group of powerful synthetic 'woody-amber' molecules.
Amberwood.history: Amberwoods became hugely popular in the 2010s, giving the dry, long-lasting trail of many modern perfumes.

Georgywood.source: A synthetic woody molecule made by Firmenich.
Georgywood.history: Developed in the 2000s as a more powerful relative of Iso E Super.
molecules: smooth, ambery-woody, a little like Iso E Super

Mystikal.source: A synthetic molecule made by Givaudan.
Mystikal.history: Developed in the 2010s to give a warm, ambery, incense-like wood.

Safraleine.source: A synthetic molecule made by Givaudan.
Safraleine.history: Created to recreate saffron's leathery side, it's now in many 'saffron' perfumes.

Ambrette.source: Distilled from the seeds of a hibiscus relative grown in Ecuador, Peru and India. It's one of the few natural plant musks.
Ambrette.history: Ambrette was used in perfumes as a plant alternative to animal musk. Its musk molecule, ambrettolide, is still prized.

Anise.source: Distilled from aniseed or star anise, mainly in China and Vietnam.
Anise.history: Anise flavoured Roman cakes and is the taste of pastis, ouzo and absinthe.

Liquorice.source: Liquorice root tastes sweet but barely smells, so the smell is recreated with anise molecules.
Liquorice.history: Liquorice root was found in Tutankhamun's tomb. Lolita Lempicka (1997) made it a perfume note.

Turmeric.source: Steam-distilled from the rhizome in India.
Turmeric.history: Turmeric has been used in India for about 4,000 years as a spice, dye and medicine.

Sesame.source: Built with molecules that smell of toasted seeds.
Sesame.history: Sesame is one of the oldest oilseed crops, grown in India over 4,000 years ago.

Hazelnut.history: Hazelnut became a popular gourmand note alongside praline and chocolate.

Maté.source: Absolute from dried leaves of the yerba maté shrub, from South America.
Maté.history: The Guaraní people drank maté long before Europeans arrived. In perfume it smells green, smoky and tobacco-like.

Paprika.source: Oleoresin extracted from dried, ground sweet peppers in Spain and Hungary.
Paprika.history: Peppers came to Europe from the Americas in the 16th century. Hungary and Spain made paprika part of their national cuisines.

Fenugreek.source: Extracted from fenugreek seeds in India.
Fenugreek.history: Fenugreek has been eaten since ancient Egypt. Its key molecule, sotolon, also gives maple syrup and curry their smell.

Costus.source: Originally from the roots of a Himalayan plant. Natural costus is now banned in perfume as an allergen, so it's recreated.
Costus.history: Costus was used in ancient Indian and Chinese medicine. In perfume it gives a strange, animalic smell of hair or wet fur.

Lavandin.source: Steam-distilled from a hybrid of true lavender and spike lavender, grown widely in Provence.
Lavandin.history: Lavandin was planted across Provence from the 1920s because it yields far more oil than true lavender. Most of the purple fields in photos are lavandin.
molecules: sharper and more herbal than true lavender

Myrtle.source: Steam-distilled from the leaves in Corsica, Morocco and Tunisia.
Myrtle.history: In ancient Greece myrtle was sacred to Aphrodite. In the 16th century 'angel water', made with myrtle, was a popular skin tonic.

Mace.source: Distilled from the red lace-like coat (aril) around the nutmeg seed.
Mace.history: Mace and nutmeg come from the same fruit. Like nutmeg, it was once worth a fortune.

Caraway.source: Steam-distilled from caraway seeds in the Netherlands and Finland.
Caraway.history: Caraway is a mirror-image puzzle: its main molecule, D-carvone, is the exact mirror image of spearmint's L-carvone, yet they smell completely different.

Pimento.source: Distilled from allspice berries, mainly in Jamaica.
Pimento.history: Spanish explorers named it after pepper (pimienta). It's called allspice because it smells like clove, cinnamon and nutmeg at once.

Angelica.source: Distilled from the roots or seeds, in Belgium, France and Hungary.
Angelica.history: Legend says the Archangel Michael revealed it as a cure for the plague. It flavours gin and Chartreuse.

Artemisia.source: Distilled from the leaves of wormwood and its relatives, around the Mediterranean.
Artemisia.history: Wormwood gave its name and bitterness to absinthe, the 'green fairy' of 19th-century Paris.

Melon.history: Melon notes became a hallmark of fresh, watery perfumes in the 1990s.

Blackberry.source: An accord of berry and cassis molecules.
Blackberry.history: L'Artisan Parfumeur's Mûre et Musc (1978) paired blackberry with musk and became a cult classic.

Nectarine.source: Recreated with lactones and fruity esters.
Nectarine.history: The nectarine is a smooth-skinned peach. In perfume it's a juicier, brighter version of peach.

Prunol.source: A historic plum 'base' (a ready-made mix) from the French firm De Laire, built mostly on fruity lactones.
Prunol.history: Prunol gave the dark plum heart to Rochas Femme (1944), created by Edmond Roudnitska.

Cucumber.source: Recreated with the same molecule that gives cucumber its smell.
Cucumber.history: Cucumber notes became popular in fresh, aquatic perfumes in the 1990s.

Milk.source: An accord built from creamy lactones.
Milk.history: Milky notes grew with the gourmand trend of the 2000s and 2010s.

Lactones.source: A family of molecules that occur naturally in fruit and dairy, mostly made synthetically.
Lactones.history: Lactones like 'C-14' (peach) and 'C-18' (coconut) have been used since the early 20th century, as in Guerlain's Mitsouko (1919).

Cream.source: An accord of lactones and vanilla.
Cream.history: Creamy notes soften gourmand and floral perfumes.

Brown Sugar.source: An accord of caramel and molasses molecules.
Brown Sugar.history: Brown sugar is a staple of modern gourmand perfumes.

Bamboo.source: Bamboo gives no oil, so it's an accord of green, watery molecules.
Bamboo.history: Bamboo became a popular note in fresh, zen-inspired perfumes from the 1990s.

Matcha.source: An accord of green tea, grassy and seaweed-like molecules.
Matcha.history: The Zen monk Eisai brought powdered tea to Japan in 1191. Matcha is grown in shade, which gives it its savoury, seaweed-like smell.

Rice.source: An accord of powdery and popcorn-like molecules.
Rice.history: Rice powder was used as face powder in Japan and China for centuries, which is why rice notes often feel powdery.
molecules: the popcorn smell of jasmine and basmati rice

Lotus.source: Lotus absolute exists (from India), but lotus notes are usually recreated.
Lotus.history: The lotus is sacred in Hinduism and Buddhism, as a symbol of purity rising from muddy water.

Pandan.source: From the leaves of the pandan plant, used across Southeast Asia. Usually an accord.
Pandan.history: Pandan is called the 'vanilla of Asia' and flavours rice and desserts.
molecules: the same popcorn-rice smell as jasmine rice

Corn.source: An accord of popcorn and sweetcorn molecules.
Corn.history: Corn was domesticated in Mexico about 9,000 years ago.

Cognac.source: Cognac oil is distilled from the wine lees left over from making cognac in France.
Cognac.history: Cognac is a brandy from the Cognac region, aged in oak. Kilian's Angels' Share (2020) made it a perfume note.

Tonalide.source: A synthetic musk made in the lab.
Tonalide.history: Tonalide is a 'polycyclic musk' from the 1950s. It's the clean, sweet musk of many laundry products, and its use is now restricted because it lingers in the environment.

Mango.source: Recreated with fruity and resinous molecules.
Mango.history: Mango comes from India, where it has been grown for over 4,000 years.

Cannabis.source: Hemp essential oil is steam-distilled from the flowering tops and contains no THC.
Cannabis.history: Hemp has been grown for fibre for thousands of years. Cannabis notes became a niche trend in the 2010s.

Guava.history: Guava comes from Central and South America.

Watermelon.history: Watermelon notes peaked with the fresh, aquatic perfumes of the 1990s.

Ginseng.history: Ginseng root has been used in Korean and Chinese medicine for over 2,000 years.

Parsley.source: Distilled from parsley leaves or seeds.
Parsley.history: The ancient Greeks wore parsley crowns at games. In perfume it adds a sharp, green, herbal twist.

Eucalyptus.source: Steam-distilled from eucalyptus leaves, in China, Portugal and Australia.
Eucalyptus.history: Joseph Bosisto started the first commercial eucalyptus oil distillery in Victoria, Australia, in 1852.
molecules: 70–85% of the oil: cool and medicinal

Citrus Notes.source: A general term for the smell of citrus peel and juice.
Citrus Notes.history: Citrus colognes are among the oldest perfumes. Farina's Eau de Cologne (1709) was built on them.

Hay.source: Hay absolute is extracted from dried grasses. Coumarin gives most of the smell.
Hay.history: Coumarin is what makes freshly dried hay smell sweet. Hay absolute is used in warm, rustic perfumes.

Honeysuckle.source: Honeysuckle gives no oil, so it's an accord.
Honeysuckle.history: Honeysuckle climbs hedges across Europe and smells strongest at dusk, to attract moths.

Moss.source: Oakmoss and treemoss (a lichen on conifers) give mossy extracts. Restricted allergens are now removed.
Moss.history: Mossy notes are the backbone of the chypre family, which began with Coty's Chypre (1917).

White Flowers.source: A bouquet accord of jasmine, tuberose, orange blossom and gardenia.
White Flowers.history: White flowers are the backbone of many feminine classics, from Fracas (1948) to modern bridal perfumes.

Red Berries.source: An accord of raspberry, strawberry and redcurrant notes.
Red Berries.history: Red berries became a staple of fruity-floral perfumes from the 1990s.

Strawberry.history: The garden strawberry was bred in 18th-century France by crossing a Chilean and a North American species.

Lychee.history: Lychee was the favourite fruit of the Tang dynasty consort Yang Guifei, and riders relayed it fresh to the capital for her.

Citron.source: Pressed from the peel of the citron, a large, thick-skinned citrus grown around the Mediterranean.
Citron.history: Citron is one of the original citrus species and was the first to reach the Mediterranean, over 2,000 years ago. It's used in the Jewish festival of Sukkot.

Verbena.source: Lemon verbena from South America. The oil is restricted because it can irritate skin, so it's often recreated.
Verbena.history: Spanish explorers brought lemon verbena to Europe in the 17th century. It's a classic of French colognes and herbal teas.

Smoke.source: An accord of smoky materials like birch tar, cade oil and guaiacol.
Smoke.history: Smoky notes recall campfires and incense. Lapsang souchong tea and smoked woods inspire many niche perfumes.

Spices.source: A general term for warm spice notes.
Spices.history: The spice trade shaped history and perfumery alike. Spicy perfumes boomed with Opium (1977).

Orcanox.history: Used to give a warm, ambergris-like effect, similar to Ambrox.

Davana.source: Steam-distilled from a small herb grown in Karnataka, India.
Davana.history: Davana is offered to the god Shiva in India. Its smell is boozy and fruity, like dried apricots in brandy.

Pittosporum.source: Pittosporum gives no oil, so its scent is an accord.
Pittosporum.history: Pittosporum hedges line Mediterranean gardens, and in spring their flowers smell like orange blossom.

Maltol.source: A molecule found in larch bark and roasted malt, mostly made synthetically.
Maltol.history: Maltol and its stronger cousin ethyl maltol made the 'candy floss' smell of gourmand perfumes possible.
molecules: candy floss, caramel and toasted malt

Datura.source: Datura is poisonous and gives no extract, so it's an accord.
Datura.history: Datura (angel's trumpet) flowers open at night with a heady, lily-like smell.

Resins.source: A general term for frankincense, myrrh, benzoin, labdanum and other tree resins.
Resins.history: Resins were among the first perfumes: 'per fumum' means 'through smoke' in Latin.

Amyris.source: Distilled from the wood of a small tree from Haiti and Jamaica.
Amyris.history: Sold as 'West Indian sandalwood', though it isn't related to sandalwood. It's a soft, cheap woody base.

Marjoram.source: Distilled from the leaves and flowers in Egypt.
Marjoram.history: Greeks crowned newlyweds with marjoram as a symbol of happiness.

Thyme.history: Egyptians used thyme in embalming and the Greeks in their baths. Its main molecule, thymol, is a natural antiseptic.

Fennel.history: Fennel was valued by Romans, and is one of the herbs in absinthe.

Cascarilla.source: Distilled from the bark of a shrub from the Bahamas.
Cascarilla.history: Cascarilla bark flavours Campari and Vermouth, and was once added to tobacco.

Ivy.source: Ivy gives no oil, so it's a green accord.
Ivy.history: Ivy was sacred to Dionysus in ancient Greece. In perfume it gives a bitter, leafy green.

Ambrettolide.source: A musk molecule found in ambrette seeds, now mostly made synthetically.
Ambrettolide.history: Identified in ambrette seed oil in the 1920s, it is one of the most prized natural-identical musks.

Bayberry.source: Bayberry (wax myrtle) grows on North America's east coast. Its scent in perfume is an accord.
Bayberry.history: Colonial Americans boiled bayberries to make fragrant wax for Christmas candles.

Marigold.source: Tagetes oil is distilled from Mexican marigold in Egypt and South Africa. Its use is restricted.
Marigold.history: Marigolds are central to Mexico's Day of the Dead. The oil smells fruity, green and apple-like.

Four O'Clock Flower.source: The flower gives no oil, so it's an accord.
Four O'Clock Flower.history: Named because its flowers open in the late afternoon. It comes from the tropical Americas.

Spun Sugar.history: Spun sugar notes are a key part of the gourmand family that began with Angel (1992).

Chestnut.source: An accord of roasted nut and sweet molecules.
Chestnut.history: Roasted chestnuts are a winter street food across Europe.

Cade.source: A tar made by heating the wood of prickly juniper, then refined.
Cade.history: Cade oil was used for centuries in skin medicine and gives a smoky, leathery note in perfumes.

Carrot Seed.source: Distilled from wild carrot seeds in France and Hungary.
Carrot Seed.history: Perfumers love carrot seed because it smells a little like iris, earthy and powdery, at a fraction of the price.

Nettle.history: Nettles were used for fibre, food and medicine across Europe.

Peach Blossom.source: Peach blossom gives no oil, so it's a soft floral-fruity accord.
Peach Blossom.history: In China peach blossom symbolises spring and love.

Tomato Leaf.source: An accord based on the smell of tomato vines.
Tomato Leaf.history: The bitter-green smell you get when brushing a tomato plant comes mainly from one molecule, isobutylthiazole.

Paradisone.source: A purified form of Hedione made by Firmenich.
Paradisone.history: Paradisone is the most powerful isomer of Hedione, about 20 times stronger.

Cetalox.source: Firmenich's name for its Ambrox molecule.
Cetalox.history: Cetalox is the brand name for Firmenich's ambroxide, created to replace ambergris.

Cachalox.source: A synthetic ambery molecule. The name nods to the cachalot, the French word for sperm whale.
Cachalox.history: Created to give an ambergris-like warmth.

Muscenone.source: A synthetic macrocyclic musk made by Firmenich.
Muscenone.history: Muscenone is close to muscone, the musk-deer molecule, and is prized for its rich, natural musk smell.

Muscone.source: The key molecule of musk-deer musk, now made synthetically.
Muscone.history: Leopold Ružička worked out its ring structure in 1926 and later won a Nobel Prize.

Exaltolide.source: A musk molecule found in angelica root, made synthetically by Firmenich.
Exaltolide.history: One of the earliest macrocyclic musks, made in the 1920s.

Exaltone.history: Ružička first made it in 1926. It was one of the first synthetic musks that resemble natural musk.

Habanolide.source: A synthetic musk made by Firmenich.
Habanolide.history: Habanolide gives a 'hot iron', clean-laundry musk to many modern perfumes.

Helvetolide.source: A synthetic musk made by Firmenich.
Helvetolide.history: Launched in the 1990s, it adds a fruity, pear-like musk.

Dreamwood.history: Made to replace scarce Indian sandalwood.

Clearwood.source: A Firmenich material made by fermentation (biotech). It smells like patchouli without the earthy darkness.
Clearwood.history: Launched in the 2010s as a 'clean' patchouli.

Vulcanolide.history: Used in modern perfumes for a warm, smoky wood.

Limbanol.history: Part of the family of dry woody-ambers popular in the 2000s and 2010s.

Woodleather.source: An accord of woods and leather.
Woodleather.history: A modern take on the leather family.

Cascalone.source: A synthetic marine molecule related to Calone.
Cascalone.history: Cascalone gives a fresh, sea-spray note, stronger and more natural than Calone.

Irone.source: The molecule that gives iris root its smell. Found in orris butter, also made synthetically.
Irone.history: Irones form slowly as iris roots dry for years, which is why orris is so costly.

Z11.history: Used in modern perfumes for a dry, ambery wood.

Chamomile.source: Distilled from chamomile flowers. German chamomile oil is blue; Roman chamomile is fruity.
Chamomile.history: Chamomile tea has been a calming remedy since ancient Egypt.
molecules: the blue colour of German chamomile

Gurjun Balsam.source: Resin tapped from tall trees in India and Southeast Asia.
Gurjun Balsam.history: Gurjun balsam is used as a soft, woody fixative.

Hawthorn.source: Hawthorn gives no oil, so it's an accord.
Hawthorn.history: Hawthorn blossom ('may') flowers in English hedgerows in May. It smells sweet and almondy.

Liatris.source: Leaves of 'deer's tongue', from the south-eastern USA.
Liatris.history: Its leaves were used to flavour pipe tobacco for their vanilla-hay smell.

White Woods.source: An accord of soft, pale, clean synthetic woods and musks.
White Woods.history: White woods became popular in the 2000s as a clean, modern wood.

Sun-Warmed Woods.source: An accord of woods and salicylates that smells like sun on skin.
Sun-Warmed Woods.history: Salicylates are also used in sunscreen, which is why they smell like summer.
